# 2026 F-1 fixed-period admission rule: current status

DHS published a final rule on July 17, 2026 that would replace the longstanding F-1 duration-of-status (D/S) admission framework with fixed periods of admission and add related requirements. It was scheduled to take effect September 15, 2026.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts first postponed the rule's effective date in September 2026. On November 16, 2026, the court granted plaintiffs' summary-judgment motion and vacated the final rule under the Administrative Procedure Act. The rule should therefore not be described as currently implemented based solely on its original effective date. The government may seek further review, so this is a time-sensitive legal development: check the latest court docket, DHS/USCIS announcements, and the school's international student office before acting.

This court ruling concerns the fixed-period rule. It does not itself decide any student's individual status, authorize employment, extend a Form I-20, or resolve other F-1 questions.

# Day 1 CPT: what the term means and what the rules require

“Day 1 CPT” is an informal phrase, not a separate visa category or a special kind of work permit. It usually describes a school-authorized Curricular Practical Training (CPT) placement that begins during the first academic year of a graduate program. Whether a particular student and job qualify depends on the program, curriculum, student history, and DSO authorization—not the program's marketing label.

## When CPT may begin during the first academic year

## When CPT may begin during the first academic year

The general rule requires an F-1 student to complete one full academic year of lawful full-time study at an approved SEVP-certified college, university, conservatory, or seminary before practical training. Federal regulation provides an exception for students enrolled in graduate studies that require immediate participation in CPT. This is a narrow, program-specific exception: a student should not assume that any graduate program, internship option, or school's Day 1 CPT policy qualifies.

Before relying on the exception, ask the DSO to explain in writing how the internship or practical training is required by, and integrated into, the established curriculum for the student's specific degree program and why the program qualifies for the graduate immediate-participation exception. A DSO's ability to enter CPT in SEVIS does not make every underlying arrangement legally eligible, and an employer's offer alone does not authorize work.

## CPT requirements that still apply

- The training must be directly related to the student's major area of study and an integral part of the school's established curriculum.
- The student must have a specific training opportunity before CPT can be authorized. The authorization is for the named employer, location, dates, and full-time or part-time basis.
- The DSO must authorize the CPT in SEVIS and issue a Form I-20 showing the authorization. The student may begin only on or after the authorized start date shown on the CPT I-20. CPT cannot be backdated.
- The student must continue to meet F-1 study and status requirements. CPT is not a general employment benefit and is not interchangeable with OPT.
- One year or more of full-time CPT makes a student ineligible for post-completion OPT at the same educational level. The student's cumulative CPT history matters, including authorization from prior schools at that same level.
## Questions to ask the school before enrolling or accepting a job

1. Is practical training required by the curriculum for this exact degree and cohort, or is it optional employment marketed as curricular?
2. Which specific course, credit, learning objective, or degree requirement makes this training integral to the curriculum?
3. Does the program require immediate CPT participation under the graduate-study exception, and what documentation supports that conclusion?
4. What enrollment, attendance, academic progress, and in-person requirements apply each term? Can the student realistically satisfy them while working?
5. What exact employer, worksite, duties, hours, and dates will appear in SEVIS and on the Form I-20? When may work legally start?
6. How will full-time or part-time CPT be calculated, and how much full-time CPT has already been used at this degree level?
7. What are the consequences for future OPT eligibility, school transfer, travel, or a later change in education level?

Get case-specific advice from the DSO before beginning work. If a program's explanation is unclear, or the student is deciding whether to enroll, an experienced immigration attorney can review the curriculum and individual circumstances. Do not begin employment while waiting for authorization.

## Short answer for common questions

**Can F-1 students do Day 1 CPT?** Sometimes a graduate student may qualify for CPT before completing one academic year if the graduate program requires immediate CPT participation and all CPT requirements are met. The phrase “Day 1 CPT” by itself does not establish eligibility. The DSO must authorize the specific training in SEVIS, and the student must have the endorsed CPT Form I-20 before working.

**Is Day 1 CPT automatically illegal?** The label alone does not decide legality. The controlling questions are whether the graduate-study exception applies, the training is genuinely integral to the established curriculum and directly related to the major, and the student and school meet all applicable requirements.

**Can I start after getting a job offer or after asking the DSO?** No. Do not begin until the DSO has authorized the specific CPT in SEVIS, issued the endorsed Form I-20, and the CPT start date has arrived.

**Does CPT affect OPT?** One year or more of full-time CPT makes the student ineligible for post-completion OPT at that educational level. Part-time CPT does not trigger that specific bar, but students should have their full CPT history reviewed by the DSO.

# F-1 work and Curricular Practical Training (CPT)

F-1 employment is limited and category-specific. Always get written guidance from your DSO before starting a job, internship, gig, volunteer role that may be employment, or other work. An employer's willingness to hire you does not establish immigration work authorization.

## On-campus employment

Eligible F-1 students may generally work on campus subject to the regulatory conditions. While school is in session, the general limit is 20 hours per week; full-time on-campus work may be allowed during official school breaks when the student is eligible and intends to register for the next term. The DSO can confirm whether a particular job and schedule qualify as on-campus employment.

## CPT

## CPT

Curricular Practical Training is employment or training that is an integral part of an established curriculum, such as a required internship, cooperative education placement, or practicum. It is authorized by the DSO in SEVIS for a specific employer, location, dates, and full-time or part-time basis. The student must receive an updated Form I-20 showing the CPT authorization before beginning work. CPT is not a general work permit and cannot be used simply because a student has found an internship.

Students generally must have completed one full academic year in valid F-1 status before CPT, except for graduate programs that require immediate participation in CPT. School and program requirements also apply. Full-time CPT totaling 12 months or more at the same educational level makes a student ineligible for post-completion OPT at that level. Part-time CPT does not trigger that particular 12-month bar.

“Day 1 CPT” is an informal label for CPT at the start of a program; it is not its own authorization category. The graduate-program exception is limited to graduate studies that require immediate CPT participation. A program's advertising or ability to enter an authorization in SEVIS does not alone establish that the student qualifies. See [Day 1 CPT: what the term means and what the rules require](day_one_cpt.md).

## Other off-campus work categories

## Other off-campus work categories

- **OPT:** Work directly related to the student's major, authorized by USCIS after a DSO recommendation and Form I-765 approval/EAD (except limited automatic extensions under specific rules). See the OPT guide.
- **STEM OPT:** A 24-month extension for qualifying students with an eligible STEM degree and a qualifying E-Verify employer; additional reporting and training-plan rules apply.
- **Severe economic hardship:** Some students may apply to USCIS for off-campus employment authorization after meeting eligibility requirements, including one academic year in F-1 status. Do not work until authorized and the EAD is effective.
- **International organization employment:** A narrow authorization category for qualifying organizations, requiring DSO and USCIS steps.

## Before accepting a role

## Before accepting a role

Ask your DSO whether the work fits an authorized category, whether a new Form I-20 or USCIS approval is needed, what the exact start date is, and what hours/employer/location limits apply. Do not start early while an application is pending. Keep authorization documents and records of employment. Contact the DSO if the employer, worksite, hours, duties, or dates change.

# F-2 dependents and F-1 reinstatement: overview

## F-2 spouse and children

An eligible F-1 student's spouse and unmarried children under 21 may qualify for F-2 classification. Each dependent generally needs their own Form I-20 from the school's DSO and must maintain the dependent status requirements. F-2 dependents are not authorized to work in the United States. Study permission is limited and depends on the dependent's age and whether study is full-time or part-time; check current regulations and consult the DSO before enrolling in a course of study. A dependent who wants to study full-time generally needs to change to an appropriate student status before beginning.

## Reinstatement after falling out of F-1 status

## Reinstatement after falling out of F-1 status

Reinstatement is a complex USCIS process, not an automatic fix. Some students who violated status may be able to ask USCIS to reinstate F-1 status by filing Form I-539, if they satisfy the regulatory criteria. Eligibility and deadlines depend on the reason and duration of the violation, the student's intent and course of study, and other facts. A DSO recommendation does not guarantee USCIS approval. Students should stop and get case-specific guidance promptly; unauthorized employment or a serious/intentional violation can bar reinstatement or have other consequences.

Do not assume that filing a reinstatement application restores F-1 status, allows employment, or makes travel safe while the request is pending. Speak with the DSO and a qualified immigration attorney about the student's particular circumstances before filing or departing.

# F-1 student status: practical basics

This guide is general information for students in F-1 academic programs. A student's DSO and the current government rules are the authoritative sources for an individual case. Immigration rules and agency procedures can change; confirm time-sensitive decisions with the DSO and USCIS.

## Before arrival and starting school

- Attend an SEVP-certified school and use the Form I-20 issued for the school and program you will attend.
- Pay the I-901 SEVIS fee when required, obtain the appropriate visa if required, and bring your passport, visa, Form I-20, and supporting documents when traveling.
- Initial F-1 students generally may enter no earlier than 30 days before the program start date on the Form I-20.
- Report to the school and DSO by the program start date and follow the school's check-in instructions. If plans change or you cannot arrive, contact the DSO before the start date.

## Maintaining status during study

## Maintaining status during study

- Enroll in and make normal progress toward the required full course of study for your school and program. The definition depends on the program and school type.
- Do not drop below a full course load, stop attending, take a leave, or change program dates without speaking with the DSO first. A DSO may authorize a reduced course load only for qualifying reasons and generally must enter the authorization in SEVIS before the student reduces the load.
- Keep the passport valid, keep the Form I-20 and SEVIS information accurate, and report address changes to the DSO promptly (the federal rule generally requires notice within 10 days).
- Work only when the specific F-1 employment category and authorization allow it. An offer letter by itself does not authorize work.
- Ask the DSO promptly about academic difficulty, medical leave, program extensions, school changes, travel, or an error in the SEVIS record.

## Duration of status and current rule update

## Duration of status and current rule update

F-1 students traditionally have been admitted for “duration of status” (D/S), meaning they may remain while pursuing the authorized program and any applicable authorized practical training and grace period, subject to the rules. DHS published a 2026 rule that would replace D/S with fixed admission dates. A federal district court entered a preliminary injunction postponing that rule and, on November 16, 2026, vacated it on summary judgment. As of this guide's review date, do not assume the fixed-date rule is in effect; check current court and DHS/USCIS updates because further proceedings or appeals may affect the legal situation.

## If something goes wrong

## If something goes wrong

Falling out of status can have serious consequences. Do not rely on an online checklist to decide whether to depart, apply for reinstatement, or continue working. Contact the DSO promptly and consider advice from a qualified immigration attorney. USCIS uses Form I-539 for eligible F-1 reinstatement requests; filing does not itself guarantee approval or employment authorization.

# F-1 transfers, travel, and grace periods

These topics depend on the student's SEVIS record, program dates, visa, and travel history. Coordinate with the DSO before changing schools, leaving the United States, or making plans near the end of a program or OPT period.

## Transfer to another school

An F-1 student may generally transfer an active SEVIS record to another SEVP-certified school. The student should first discuss the plan with the current school's DSO, obtain admission and a transfer Form I-20 from the new school, and agree with the DSOs on a SEVIS release date. The new school must complete the required SEVIS registration and the student must begin attendance by the applicable next session/start date. A transfer during OPT can end OPT authorization, so do not transfer or change programs without confirming the effect with both DSOs.

## Changing education level or extending a program

## Changing education level or extending a program

Students moving to a new educational level or beginning a new program need a new Form I-20 and timely SEVIS updates. If more time is needed to complete the current program, contact the DSO before the program end date; a program extension generally must be requested before that date and requires an academic reason and updated funding information. Do not wait until the I-20 end date has passed.

## International travel and return

## International travel and return

Before departing, ask the DSO to confirm that the SEVIS record is in the right status and that the Form I-20 has a valid travel endorsement. For reentry, travelers commonly need a valid passport, a valid F-1 visa unless visa-exempt, and the endorsed Form I-20, plus any documents relevant to their current activity (such as an EAD and current employment evidence during OPT). A visa allows a person to seek entry; U.S. Customs and Border Protection decides admission at the port of entry. A visa expiration while inside the United States does not by itself mean the person must immediately leave, but a new visa is generally needed to return after international travel if no exception applies.

Travel while an OPT or STEM OPT application is pending, after a status violation, with an expired visa, or near a program transition can carry additional risk. Get individualized guidance before booking or departing.

## 60-day grace period

## 60-day grace period

Under the longstanding F-1 framework, students who successfully complete their program, and students whose authorized post-completion OPT ends, generally have a 60-day grace period to prepare to depart, transfer, or take another permitted step. The grace period is not employment authorization. It does not generally apply after a status violation or an early withdrawal/termination; contact the DSO immediately if studies end unexpectedly.

The DHS 2026 rule that proposed fixed admission dates was vacated by a federal district court on November 16, 2026. Its proposed stay and grace-period changes should not be presented as current law without checking for new court or agency action.

, an important initial step to reform the H-1B nonimmigrant visa program. Under the Proclamation, certain H-1B petitions filed at or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern on Sept. 21, 2025, must be accompanied by an additional $100,000 payment as a condition of eligibility.
Who is subject to the $100,000 payment:
The Proclamation applies to certain H-1B petitions filed at or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern on Sept. 21, 2025, on behalf of beneficiaries who are outside the United States and do not have a valid H-1B visa. The Proclamation also applies if a petition filed at or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern on September 21, 2025, requests consular notification, port of entry notification, or pre-flight inspection for an alien in the United States.

In addition, if a petition filed at or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern  on Sept. 21, 2025, requests a change of status or amendment or extension of stay and USCIS determines that the alien is ineligible for a change of status or an amendment or extension of stay (for example, is not in a valid nonimmigrant visa status or if the alien departs the United States prior to adjudication of a change of status request), the Proclamation will apply and the payment must be paid according to the instructions provided by USCIS.
The Proclamation does not apply to any previously issued and currently valid H-1B visas, or any petitions submitted prior to 12:01 a.m. Eastern on Sept. 21, 2025. In addition, the Proclamation does not prevent any holder of a current H-1B visa, or any alien beneficiary following petition approval, from traveling in and out of the United States.

The Proclamation also does not apply to a petition filed at or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern on Sept. 21, 2025, that is requesting an amendment, change of status, or extension of stay for an alien inside the United States where the alien is granted such amendment, change, or extension. Further, an alien beneficiary of such petition will not be considered to be subject to the payment if he or she subsequently departs the United States and applies for a visa based on the approved petition and/or seeks to reenter the United States on a current H-1B visa.

# F-1 Optional Practical Training (OPT)

OPT is temporary employment authorization for practical training directly related to an F-1 student's major field of study. OPT is not automatic: eligibility, timing, the DSO's SEVIS recommendation, USCIS adjudication, and the EAD dates all matter.

## Types

- **Pre-completion OPT** takes place before the program end date. It may be part-time while school is in session and full-time during eligible breaks. Time used is deducted from the usual 12-month allotment.
- **Post-completion OPT** takes place after completion of the program. Eligible students may generally receive up to 12 months at each higher educational level, reduced by applicable prior OPT and affected by full-time CPT of 12 months or more at that level.
- Qualifying STEM degree holders may apply for a separate 24-month STEM OPT extension; see the STEM OPT guide.

If you are finishing a second master's, eligibility depends on prior OPT and CPT use at the master's level. A second degree at the same educational level does not automatically reset the 12-month allowance. See [OPT after a second master's degree](second_masters_opt.md).

## Applying for post-completion OPT

## Applying for post-completion OPT

1. Ask the DSO to review eligibility and enter the OPT recommendation in SEVIS.
2. Obtain the updated Form I-20 showing the recommendation and check it for accuracy.
3. File Form I-765 in the correct category with USCIS within the filing window. Current Form I-765 instructions say post-completion OPT may be filed up to 90 days before the program end date and no later than 60 days after it; USCIS must receive it within 30 days of the DSO recommendation. Confirm deadlines in the current form instructions and with the DSO.
4. Wait for USCIS approval and the EAD. Do not begin work before the EAD's validity start date.
5. Keep employment directly related to the major and report employment and address changes to the DSO as required.

An application receipt notice is not an EAD and ordinarily does not authorize a new OPT job. Limited automatic work extensions can apply in specifically defined situations; confirm the exact category and current policy rather than assuming an extension applies.

## Employment and unemployment

Post-completion OPT work must be directly related to the major. Students on regular post-completion OPT may generally accrue no more than 90 days of unemployment during the OPT authorization period. Employment must meet the applicable definition and be reported in the required manner through the school/SEVIS process. Ask the DSO how to document the relationship between duties and the major, start/end dates, and any self-employment or multiple-employer arrangements.

## Travel and changes

## Travel and changes

Travel, transfer to another school, or changing education level may affect an OPT request or authorization. Ask the DSO before taking action. Keep copies of the EAD, Form I-20, passport, visa, and current employment evidence when relevant to travel.

# OPT after a second master's degree

Whether someone can receive post-completion OPT after a second master's depends mainly on the person's prior OPT use at the master's educational level, plus the current degree and F-1 eligibility requirements. A second master's does not automatically create a fresh 12-month OPT allowance.

## General rule

Federal regulations allow up to 12 months of practical training and provide eligibility for another 12 months when a student advances to a higher educational level. A master's degree is one educational level. Therefore:

- **No prior post-completion OPT used at the master's level:** The student may have OPT eligibility remaining after finishing a second master's, if all other requirements are satisfied. A second master's by itself is not a new higher educational level, so it does not independently reset the 12-month allowance.
- **Some master's-level OPT already used:** The remaining amount, if any, may be limited by the student's previous practical-training history. The student should have the DSO review every prior OPT period, SEVIS record, and EAD at that educational level.
- **A full 12 months of master's-level OPT already used:** A second master's generally does not provide a new post-completion OPT period at the same educational level. Moving to a higher educational level, such as a doctorate, may create a new 12-month practical-training allotment, subject to eligibility.

- **Full-time CPT history:** One year or more of full-time CPT at the same educational level can make the student ineligible for post-completion OPT at that level, even if they did not use post-completion OPT after the first master's.

These are general rules, not an individual eligibility decision. “Second master's” can describe different school, degree, transfer, and prior-status histories. The DSO must assess the student's full record and enter the recommendation in SEVIS; USCIS adjudicates the Form I-765.

## STEM OPT questions

A separate 24-month STEM OPT extension is not guaranteed by earning a second master's. A qualifying STEM degree, current post-completion OPT, eligible E-Verify employer, and the required Form I-983 and filing steps are needed. Regulations permit a later STEM OPT extension only within the lifetime limit and, for a second extension, it must be based on a degree at a higher level than the degree used for the first extension. Some students may be able to rely on a previously earned STEM degree for an extension, subject to detailed requirements; ask the DSO to review the degree, CIP code, timing, employer, and prior STEM OPT history.

## Changes that can affect current OPT

Starting a new degree program, transferring schools, or changing education level can affect or automatically terminate existing OPT authorization. Do not enroll, transfer, travel, or start work based on assumptions about how a pending or approved OPT period will be treated. Ask the current and new school's DSOs to confirm the exact SEVIS release date and effect on work authorization before acting.

Terms and Conditions for Employer Participation

The Employer’s Training Obligation

The Employer’s Training Obligation
As noted above, to be eligible to employ a STEM OPT student, an employer must have and maintain a bona fide employer-employee relationship with the student. The employer must attest to this fact by signing the Form I-983, Training Plan for STEM OPT Students. To establish a bona fide relationship, the employer may not be the student’s “employer” in name only, nor may the student work for the employer on a “volunteer” basis. Moreover, the employer that signs the Form I-983 must be the same entity that provides the practical training experience to the student.

An employer must have sufficient resources and trained or supervisory personnel available to provide appropriate training in connection with the specified training opportunity at the location(s) where the student’s practical training experience will take place, as specified in the Form I-983. The “personnel” who may provide and supervise the training experience may be either employees of the employer, or contractors who the employer has directly retained to provide services to the employer; they may not, however, be employees or contractors of the employer’s clients or customers. Additionally, under no circumstances would another F-1 student with OPT or a STEM OPT extension (who is undergoing training in their own right) be qualified to train another F-1 student with a STEM OPT extension.

While employers may rely on their existing training programs or policies to satisfy the requirements relating to performance evaluation and oversight and supervision, the student’s Training Plan must nevertheless be customized for the individual student. For instance, every Training Plan must describe the direct relationship between the STEM OPT opportunity and the student’s qualifying STEM degree, as well as the relationship between the STEM OPT opportunity and the student’s goals and objectives for work-based learning. Moreover, a STEM OPT employer may not assign, or otherwise delegate, its training responsibilities to a non-employer third party (such as a client/customer of the employer, employees of the client/customer, or contractors of the client/customer).

As noted above, DHS, at its discretion, may conduct a site visit of any STEM OPT employer to ensure that the employer possesses and maintains the ability and resources to provide structured and guided work-based learning experiences consistent with the Form I-983. See 8 C.F.R. 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C)(11). Consistent with this provision, during a site visit, DHS may verify that the employer that signs Form I-983 is the same entity that provides the practical training experience to the student and ensure compliance. For ICE to effectively conduct these site visits as part of its oversight responsibilities, it is important that employers report any change in a student’s employment address. As indicated above, the employer and student must report such a material change by submitting a modified Form I-983 to the DSO at the earliest available opportunity.
The Employer’s Training Obligation: Staffing and Temporary Agencies

Staffing and temporary agencies and consulting firms may seek to employ students under the STEM OPT program, but only if they will be the entity that provides the practical training experience to the student and they have and maintain a bona fide employer-employee relationship with the student. STEM OPT participants may engage in a training experience that takes place at a site other than the employer’s principal place of business as long as all of the training obligations are met, including that the employer has and maintains a bona fide employer-employee relationship with the student. Certain types of arrangements, including multiple employer arrangements, sole proprietorships, employment through ‘‘temp’’ agencies, employment through consulting firm arrangements that provide labor for hire, and other similar relationships may not be able to demonstrate a bona fide employer-employee relationship and, therefore, may not meet the requirements of the STEM OPT extension.

As part of the STEM OPT extension, employers must complete the appropriate parts of Form I-983, Training Plan for STEM OPT Students. In this form, employers attest that:
They have enough resources and trained personnel available to appropriately train the student;
The student will not replace a full- or part-time, temporary or permanent U.S. worker; and
Working for them will help the student attain their training objectives.
DHS will review on a case-by-case basis whether the student will be a bona fide employee of the employer signing the training plan, and verify that the employer that signs the training plan, is the same entity that employs the student and provides the practical training experience.

# F-1 24-month STEM OPT extension

The STEM OPT extension is a 24-month extension of post-completion OPT for eligible F-1 students. It has additional degree, employer, training-plan, reporting, and timing requirements. Confirm eligibility with the DSO and current USCIS instructions before relying on any deadline.

## Core eligibility points

## Core eligibility points

- The student must be in a valid period of post-completion OPT and have a qualifying bachelor's, master's, or doctoral degree in a field on the current DHS STEM Designated Degree Program List. The relevant degree may, in some circumstances, be a previously earned STEM degree from an appropriately accredited and SEVP-certified U.S. institution.
- The job must be directly related to the qualifying STEM degree and meet the training-program requirements.
- The employer must be enrolled in E-Verify and have an employer-employee relationship that meets the rules. The employer must be able to complete and sign Form I-983 and comply with its training and reporting obligations.
- Each qualifying employer must provide at least 20 hours of work per week. Unemployment limits and the cumulative limits for regular OPT plus STEM OPT apply.

## Application process and timing

## Application process and timing

1. Work with the DSO to confirm the degree/CIP code, employer, and proposed training plan.
2. Complete and sign Form I-983 with the employer; submit it to the DSO as directed. The DSO makes the STEM OPT recommendation in SEVIS and issues an updated Form I-20.
3. File Form I-765 with USCIS in the STEM category in the current filing window. Current instructions generally allow filing up to 90 days before the current OPT EAD expires; a separate deadline applies after the DSO's recommendation is entered. Check the latest I-765 instructions and DSO guidance for the exact filing deadline.
4. If a timely STEM OPT extension application is pending when the current EAD expires, a temporary automatic extension of employment authorization may apply under the regulations, generally for up to 180 days while the application is pending. Verify that the filing and eligibility conditions are met before working under this provision.

## Ongoing duties

## Ongoing duties

- Report required changes to the DSO within the applicable deadlines, including address, employer, employment dates, and material changes to the training plan.
- Complete required validation reports with the DSO, commonly at 6-month intervals, and submit the required I-983 evaluations (including the midpoint and final evaluation) on time.
- Work with the employer to update or replace the I-983 if material training or employer details change. Keep the signed training plan, evaluations, pay records, and evidence that the work relates to the STEM degree.
- Keep total unemployment within the allowed combined limit for OPT and STEM OPT. Contact the DSO if a job ends or a new employer is involved.

H-1B Cap
The H-1B classification has an annual numerical limit (cap) of 65,000 new statuses or visas each fiscal year (with certain deductions and additions based on H-1B1 set asides and usage). An additional 20,000 petitions filed on behalf of beneficiaries who have earned a master’s degree or higher from a U.S. institution of higher education are exempt from the cap. Additionally, H-1B workers who are petitioned for or employed at an institution of higher education or its affiliated or related nonprofit entities, a nonprofit research organization, or a government research organization, are not subject to this numerical cap.

Changing Employers
When can I begin working for a new H-1B employer if I change employers?
If you are changing H-1B employers, you may begin working for the new employer as soon as they properly file a non-frivolous Form I-129 petition on your behalf, or as of the requested start date on that petition, whichever is later.
To be eligible for portability, you must not have been employed without authorization from the time of your last admission into the United States, and your new employer must properly file a new, non-frivolous petition before your H-1B period of authorized stay expires.
Will I still have employment authorization if I change employers?
If you are eligible for H-1B portability, your employment is authorized until USCIS has made a decision on the Form I-129.

Will I still have employment authorization if I change employers?
If you are eligible for H-1B portability, your employment is authorized until USCIS has made a decision on the Form I-129.
If the new I-129 petition is approved, you may continue working for the new employer for the period of time indicated on the new petition approval.
If the new petition is denied, you may continue working for your previous employer if your prior period of authorized employment is still valid, but your authorization to work based on portability ceases upon denial of the petition.
If you are laid off, fired, quit, or otherwise cease employment with your previous employer, you may have up to 60 consecutive days or until the end of your authorized validity period, whichever is shorter, to find new employment, change status, or depart the country.

If you are currently employed in a cap-exempt position, you may engage in concurrent employment in a cap-subject position as long as you will continue to be employed in the cap-exempt position. You may begin working concurrently for the cap-subject employer as soon as they properly file a non-frivolous Form I-129 petition on your behalf, or as of the requested start date on that petition, whichever is later. As long as you continue your cap-exempt employment, were previously counted toward the cap, or otherwise remain cap exempt, you will not become subject to the H-1B cap again during the same H-1B validity period.
